title: Do not infer domain exception classes from a transport status alone
applies_when: Aligning local and remote SDK exception behavior or converting structured HTTP errors across Rust and Python/Node bindings.
lesson: Trace the server envelope, transport variant and language bridge separately. Test two different domain failures sharing a status/code, malformed bodies and non-target statuses. Preserve request ID, status, cause and body when changing classification. HTTP 400 or an application code is not a domain enum unless its documented contract distinguishes the relevant failures; blanket ValueError inheritance or message substring matching can misclassify conflicts and hide diagnostics.
avoid_when: A versioned server contract may provide an unambiguous typed discriminator; test and use that instead. Synthetic native HTTP mocks establish client behavior, not live-server semantics or cross-language runtime qualification. A confirmed parity gap can remain real even when a proposed broad repair is unsafe. Team-input issues need a contract decision, not automatic rejection or a competing speculative PR.

evidence.note: Reported local invalid-input ValueError and tag-conflict RuntimeError both arrive remotely as HttpError with HTTP400/code13. This is an issue report asking for team input, not our live Cloud measurement.

check_response retains unsuccessful response text, request ID and status in Error::Http. The accompanying repository example exercises this unchanged native client with four synthetic diagnostic cases, not a repaired server.
The bridge maps Http to HttpError and InvalidInput to ValueError. Native Rust mock results do not qualify a rebuilt PyO3 package.
InvalidInput carries only message, unlike Http's request_id/status/source; a direct variant swap would lose diagnostics unless the contract is redesigned.
